content: Norethindrone acetate and ethinyl estradiol are a combination of hormonal agents used as oral contraceptives. They are FDA-approved for several indications, including contraception, treatment of acne in women who also desire contraception, management of moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms associated with menopause, and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis in women with an intact uterus. Common Adverse Reactions: Patients may experience abdominal cramps, abdominal pain, bloating, nausea, headaches, breakthrough bleeding, and breast pain as common side effects. Adult Indications and Dosage: 1. Contraception: These tablets are indicated for the prevention of pregnancy in women who choose oral contraceptives as their method of contraception. Oral contraceptives are highly effective when used correctly and consistently. The failure rate is lower with proper adherence to the prescribed regimen. The tablets are arranged in a dispenser with three rows of seven tablets each, labeled with the days of the week to facilitate adherence. Two initiation regimens are available: Sunday-Start Regimen: The first tablet is taken on the first Sunday after menstrual flow begins. If menstruation starts on a Sunday, the first tablet is taken that same day. Tablets are taken daily for 21 consecutive days, followed by a 7-day tablet-free interval. Day-1 Start Regimen: The first tablet is taken on the first day of menstrual flow. Tablets are taken daily for 21 consecutive days, followed by a 7-day tablet-free interval. Patients should use an additional method of contraception during the first week of the initial cycle. Tablets should be taken at the same time each day, preferably with a meal or at bedtime, to maximize efficacy. 2. Acne-Contraception: One tablet is taken orally daily for 21 consecutive days, followed by a 7-day tablet-free interval. 3. Menopause (Moderate to Severe Vasomotor Symptoms): Therapy should begin at the lowest effective dose and for the shortest duration consistent with treatment goals and risks. One tablet is taken orally daily. 4. Postmenopausal Osteoporosis Prevention: Therapy should also start at the lowest effective dose and for the shortest duration. One tablet is taken orally daily. Effects on Menstrual Cycle: Increased regularity of menstrual cycles. Reduced blood loss and decreased incidence of iron-deficiency anemia. Decreased incidence of dysmenorrhea. Effects Related to Ovulation Inhibition: Reduced incidence of functional ovarian cysts. Decreased risk of ectopic pregnancies. Long-Term Use Benefits: Lower incidence of fibroadenomas and fibrocystic breast disease. Reduced risk of acute pelvic inflammatory disease. Decreased risk of endometrial and ovarian cancers. Contraindications: Oral contraceptives should not be used in women with the following conditions: Thrombophlebitis or thromboembolic disorders. History of deep vein thrombophlebitis or thromboembolic disorders. Cerebral vascular or coronary artery disease. Known or suspected breast carcinoma. Carcinoma of the endometrium or other estrogen-dependent neoplasia. Undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding. Cholestatic jaundice of pregnancy or jaundice with prior pill use. Hepatic adenomas or carcinomas. Known or suspected pregnancy. Warnings: 1. Cardiovascular Risks: Oral contraceptives are associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction, thromboembolism, stroke, and other vascular problems, particularly in women with underlying risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, and diabetes. Smoking significantly increases the risk of cardiovascular events, especially in women over 35 years of age. Practitioners should carefully evaluate the cardiovascular risk profile of patients before prescribing oral contraceptives. 2. Thromboembolic Disorders: There is a well-established increased risk of thromboembolic and thrombotic events with oral contraceptive use. The risk is not related to the duration of use and disappears after discontinuation. Oral contraceptives should be discontinued at least four weeks prior to and for two weeks after elective surgery associated with increased thromboembolic risk or during prolonged immobilization. 3. Cerebrovascular Events: Oral contraceptives increase the risk of thrombotic and hemorrhagic strokes, particularly in older women who smoke and have hypertension. 4. Hepatic Neoplasia: Benign hepatic adenomas are associated with oral contraceptive use, though rare. Long-term use may increase the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. 5. Gallbladder Disease: Earlier studies suggested an increased risk of gallbladder disease, but more recent data indicate minimal risk with lower-dose formulations. 6. Carbohydrate and Lipid Metabolism: Oral contraceptives may cause glucose intolerance and hyperinsulinism, particularly with higher estrogen doses. Women with prediabetes or diabetes should be monitored closely. 7. Elevated Blood Pressure: Oral contraceptives can increase blood pressure, particularly in older users or with prolonged use. Blood pressure typically returns to normal after discontinuation. 8. Headaches: New or worsening migraines or severe headaches require discontinuation and evaluation. 9. Bleeding Irregularities: Breakthrough bleeding and spotting may occur, especially during the first three months of use. Persistent or recurrent bleeding should be evaluated to rule out malignancy or pregnancy. Precautions: Oral contraceptives do not protect against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. Annual physical examinations, including blood pressure monitoring and cervical cytology, are recommended for all women using oral contraceptives. Use During Pregnancy: Oral contraceptives should not be used during pregnancy. If pregnancy is confirmed, the medication should be discontinued immediately. This detailed information highlights the importance of individualized patient assessment and counseling when prescribing oral contraceptives.
